clue.text: They're not designed to do superficial damage

definitions.text: They're not designed to do superficial damage

parts.words: They're not designed to do superficial damage
parts.note: weapons that explode deep under water rather than at the surface, so their damage is literally not superficial

explanation.surface: Someone insists a group of people or measures mean real harm, not just cosmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superficial' reads as 'trivial', but here it means 'at the surface': these anti-submarine weapons are set to go off far below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Anti-submarine bombs are set to detonate at a chosen depth under the sea, not on the surface.

clue.text: Bunyan as a self-confessed visionary

parts.note: John Bunyan tells The Pilgrim's Progress as a dream he had, 'I dreamed a dream'

explanation.surface: The Puritan writer admitting he sees visions.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pilgrim's Progress opens with Bunyan saying he lay down in a den, slept and dreamed: the whole book is framed as his vision.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunyan presents his allegory as something seen while asleep, making him a sleeper with visions.

clue.text: School books not necessarily first editions

definitions.text: School books not necessarily first editions

parts.words: School books not necessarily first editions
parts.note: elementary textbooks give the first lessons, but need not be a book's first printing

explanation.surface: Textbooks for the classroom that may not be valuable originals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first editions' suggests collectors' copies; the books are first only in teaching the basics.
explanation.definitionFit: Primers are elementary textbooks for beginning readers or learners.

clue.text: Gatherings: of sunny days?

parts.note: piles built up in fine weather, after the proverb about making hay while the sun shines

explanation.surface: Parties held when the weather is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gatherings' looks like social events; here it means the cut grass gathered into piles on dry, sunny days.
explanation.definitionFit: Stacks of dried grass are gathered in after mowing in sunny weather.

clue.text: Johnson's rustic cat

parts.note: Dr Samuel Johnson's cat had a name that was also old slang for a farm labourer

explanation.surface: A country cat owned by a man called Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Samuel Johnson, the 18th-century dictionary maker, kept a cat he fed oysters; its name was also a stock word for an English farmhand.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the lexicographer's cat doubles as a traditional term for a country labourer.

clue.text: Concerning a code displayed by penitents

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
Morse is the dot-and-dash telegraph code

explanation.surface: Regarding a secret cipher used by people doing penance.
explanation.definitionFit: Penitents show deep regret for what they have done wrong.

clue.text: Not a terminus of the Orient Express

definitions.text: Not a terminus of the Orient Express

parts.words: Not a terminus of the Orient Express
parts.note: read Orient as the east: an end of the east that is a London district, not a railway station

explanation.surface: A remark about where the famous luxury train does not stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the area of London east of the City; 'Orient Express' suggests the train, but 'Orient' just means east.
explanation.definitionFit: The part of London east of the old City wall is literally the eastern end.

clue.text: His customers know when he's getting slack in his business

definitions.text: His customers know when he's getting slack in his business

parts.words: His customers know when he's getting slack in his business
parts.note: slack is coal dust, so a fuel dealer handing out slack gives poor value

explanation.surface: Shoppers can tell when a tradesman starts to slack off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slack' reads as idle, but slack is also fine coal dust, which a dealer might pass off on buyers.
explanation.definitionFit: The trader sells household fuel by the sack, and slack is its cheapest dusty grade.

clue.text: Do as told about its remedy -eat less

definitions.text: Do as told about its remedy -eat less

indicators.note: the obeying word goes about, that is around, the other letters

parts.note: to do as you are told is to obey

indicators.note: to remedy is to put right or fix, so the letters of its are rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor's order: follow instructions on the cure for your condition and cut down on food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remedy' rearranges ITS into SIT, and 'about' puts SIT inside OBEY. Read as a whole, the clue describes the condition whose cure is eating less.
explanation.definitionFit: Being badly overweight is the condition a diet of smaller meals is meant to cure.

clue.text: Humble-sounding estate

indicators.note: the clue says the answer only sounds like the humbling word, a signal that it is heard rather than seen

parts.note: to humble someone is to demean them

explanation.surface: A modest-looking country property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humble-sounding' looks like a description of a plain estate; instead the answer is pronounced like DEMEAN (to humble).
explanation.definitionFit: A demesne is land held and worked by a lord, his own landed property.

clue.text: They earn interest in a roundabout and amusing way

definitions.text: They earn interest in a roundabout and amusing way

indicators.note: a roundabout way is indirect, so the letters of earn interest go round to a new order

explanation.surface: A remark about investors who make returns by unusual and entertaining means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a roundabout' rearranges EARN INTEREST; as a whole, performers earn our interest by amusing us.
explanation.definitionFit: Performers hold an audience's attention by amusing it.

clue.text: Mary's follower broke net, gets licking

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Mary had a little lamb, which followed her to school

indicators.note: the net is broken up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mary's little pet tears through a net and gets a beating for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' turns NET into ENT. 'Licking' looks like a beating in the surface, but it is the old sense of flames licking, playing lightly over a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes flame or light that plays softly over something, flickering like a tongue.

clue.text: Serious listener with a comfortable home.

parts.note: the ear is the organ that listens
a nest is a snug, cosy home

explanation.surface: A grave person who hears others out, living somewhere cosy.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest means sincere and grave in intention, not joking.

clue.text: They hold court in London, for show

definitions.text: They hold court in London, for show

parts.words: They hold court in London, for show
parts.note: noblemen who 'hold' the name of a London district, ... Court, once home to a big exhibition hall for shows

explanation.surface: Grandees hold court in the capital just for appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: Earls Court is a district of London whose exhibition centre hosted trade shows; 'hold court' reads as presiding, but the nobles own the court in the place name.
explanation.definitionFit: These peers of the realm give their name to a London district and its former exhibition venue.

clue.text: The one in dispute

parts.note: a rival who disputes, or contends, for a prize or title

explanation.definitionFit: A rival is someone who competes, taking part in a contest for a title.

clue.text: Homer motivated by this feeling ?

parts.note: a homer is a homing pigeon or anyone heading home, driven by longing for home; the poet Homer wrote of Odysseus's homesickness

explanation.surface: Wondering what emotion drove the Greek poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homer' looks like the poet but is anything that homes; the feeling has the Greek roots for 'return home' and 'pain'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word first meant homesickness, an aching wish to get back home.

clue.text: Champions of the workers rather than map-makers

definitions.text: Champions of the workers rather than map-makers

parts.words: Champions of the workers rather than map-makers
parts.note: a nineteenth-century movement for working men's rights, named after its People's Charter, not people who draw charts

explanation.surface: Defenders of labour, as opposed to cartographers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chartists were a British reform movement of the 1830s-40s that campaigned for votes for working men; the name looks as if it means chart-makers.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1830s British reformers took their name from the People's Charter demanding the vote for working men.

clue.text: One appears to put an end to it

definitions.text: One appears to put an end to it

parts.words: One appears to put an end to it
parts.note: the state of being away ends when someone shows up

explanation.surface: Someone shows up to stop something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears' reads as 'seems'; here it means turns up, which ends a person's being away.
explanation.definitionFit: Being away is ended the moment the missing person turns up.

clue.text: The dog to be in the wrong in a row

indicators.note: the being wrong sits in, that is inside, the row

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
to err is to be in the wrong

explanation.surface: A pet in trouble for misbehaving in a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' (the second) puts ERR inside TIER.
explanation.definitionFit: The terrier is a breed of small, plucky dog bred to go to earth after prey.

clue.text: Browning's girl appears good at exams

definitions.text: Browning's girl appears good at exams

parts.words: Browning's girl appears good at exams
parts.note: Robert Browning's verse drama is named for a girl who passes, so a girl who passes looks like a good examinee

explanation.surface: A girl in a Victorian poet's work seems to be a strong student.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning's poem 'Pippa Passes' follows a mill girl passing through a town; passing an exam is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the Victorian poet's verse play is a silk-mill girl who 'passes' through the town.

clue.text: Father's period of recreation

parts.note: Pa is father, so Father's gives PA'S
a period is a spell of time

explanation.surface: Dad's spell of leisure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastime is a hobby or amusement done for pleasure.

clue.text: Dowered fairy of the mineral kingdom

parts.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian mythology
a dot is a dowry, so a dowered fairy is a peri with a dot

explanation.surface: A fairy given a dowry, belonging to the realm of minerals.
explanation.walkthrough: Dot, from French, is a dowry; the fairy with one comes second in the answer, a peri followed by a dot.
explanation.definitionFit: The green gemstone is a form of olivine, a member of the mineral world.

clue.text: Declares the dullards to be about right

indicators.note: the dullards are to be around, that is outside, the other letters

parts.note: asses are fools, slow-witted people

explanation.surface: Someone states that the dim are roughly correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be about' puts RT inside ASSES.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert is to state firmly, to declare something is so.

clue.text: It's not much of a fight

explanation.definitionFit: Scrap means both a small fragment of something and an informal brawl.

clue.text: He's out of place, as a matter of course

definitions.text: He's out of place, as a matter of course

parts.words: He's out of place, as a matter of course
parts.note: a horse that fails to be placed in a race on a racecourse; 'as a matter of course' hides the racecourse

explanation.surface: Someone who naturally never fits in anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing, being 'placed' means finishing in the first few; a runner that does not is one of the many unplaced finishers on the course.
explanation.definitionFit: Also-rans are the runners that finish unplaced in a race, and by extension failures.

clue.text: Moroccan city in great disorder

indicators.note: the words in great are in disorder, so their letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A North African town is in a terrible mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorder' rearranges IN GREAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangier is a port in northern Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar.

clue.text: One in great demand by the Pied Piper.

definitions.text: One in great demand by the Pied Piper

parts.words: One in great demand by the Pied Piper
parts.note: the Piper demanded a thousand of these Dutch coins from Hamelin's mayor for ridding the town of rats

explanation.surface: Someone very popular with the legendary rat-catcher of Hamelin.
explanation.walkthrough: In Browning's poem the Pied Piper is promised a thousand of these old Dutch coins and is cheated of them; 'One' looks like a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Dutch coin was the fee the Piper asked of the town council.

clue.text: He is sure to succeed if he survives

definitions.text: He is sure to succeed if he survives

parts.words: He is sure to succeed if he survives
parts.note: the next in line to a throne or title, whose right to inherit cannot be overturned provided he outlives the holder

explanation.surface: A man whose success is guaranteed as long as he stays alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'succeed' reads as 'do well', but means 'take over a title'.
explanation.definitionFit: The next in line to a throne whose claim cannot be displaced by a later birth.
